{{short description|Well-quasi-ordering of finite trees}}
{{Redirect|TREE|the plant form|Tree||Tree (disambiguation)}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Kruskal's tree theorem''' states that the set of finite [[tree (graph theory)|tree]]s over a [[well-quasi-ordering|well-quasi-ordered]] set of labels is itself well-quasi-ordered under [[homeomorphism (graph theory)|homeomorphic]] embedding.

A [[finitary]] application of the theorem gives the existence of a fast-growing '''TREE function'''. TREE(3) is one of the largest simply defined finite numbers, dwarfing other [[large numbers]] such as [[Graham's number]] and [[googolplex]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-10-20 |title=The Enormity of the Number TREE(3) Is Beyond Comprehension |url=https://www.popularmechanics.com/science/math/a28725/number-tree3/ |access-date=2025-02-04 |website=Popular Mechanics |language=en-US}}</ref>

==History==
The [[theorem]] was [[conjecture]]d by [[Andrew Vázsonyi]] and [[mathematical proof|proved]] by {{harvs|txt=yes|year= 1960 |authorlink=Joseph Kruskal|last=Kruskal|first=Joseph}}; a short proof was given by {{harvs|txt=yes|year= 1963|authorlink=Crispin St. J. A. Nash-Williams|last=Nash-Williams|first=Crispin}}. It has since become a prominent example in [[reverse mathematics]] as a statement that cannot be proved in ATR<sub>0</sub> (a [[second-order arithmetic]] theory with a form of [[arithmetical transfinite recursion]]).

In 2004, the result was generalized from trees to [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]]s as the [[Robertson–Seymour theorem]], a result that has also proved important in reverse mathematics and leads to the even-faster-growing [[Friedman's SSCG function|SSCG function]], which dwarfs TREE.

==Statement==
The version given here is that proven by Nash-Williams; Kruskal's formulation is somewhat stronger. All trees we consider are finite.

Given a tree <math>T</math> with a [[rooted tree|root]], and given vertices <math>v</math>, <math>w</math>, call <math>w</math> a ''descendant'' of <math>v</math> if the unique path from the root to <math>w</math> contains <math>v</math>, and call <math>w</math> a ''child'' of <math>v</math> if additionally the path from <math>v</math> to <math>w</math> contains no other vertex.

Take <math>(X, \le_X)</math> to be a [[partially ordered set]]. If <math>T_1</math>, <math>T_2</math> are rooted trees with vertices labeled in <math>X</math>, we say that <math>T_1</math> is ''inf-embeddable'' in <math>T_2</math> and write <math>T_1 \leq T_2</math> if there is an [[injective map]] <math>F</math> from the vertices of <math>T_1</math> to the vertices of <math>T_2</math> such that:

*For all vertices <math>v</math> of <math>T_1</math>, the label of <math>v</math> is <math>\le_X</math> the label of <math>F(v)</math>;
*If <math>w</math> is any descendant of <math>v</math> in <math>T_1</math>, then <math>F(w)</math> is a descendant of <math>F(v)</math>; and
*If <math>w_1</math>, <math>w_2</math> are any two distinct children of <math>v</math>, then the path from <math>F(w_1)</math> to <math>F(w_2)</math> in <math>T_2</math> contains <math>F(v)</math> (equivalently, <math>F(w_1)</math> and <math>F(w_2)</math> lie in different subtrees of <math>v</math>).

Kruskal's tree theorem then states:

:If <math>X</math> is [[well-quasi-ordering|well-quasi-ordered]], then the set of rooted trees with labels in <math>X</math> is well-quasi-ordered under the inf-embeddable order defined above. That is to say, given any infinite sequence <math>T_1, T_2, \ldots</math> of rooted trees labeled in <math>X</math>, there is some <math>i<j</math> so that <math>T_i \leq T_j</math>.

==Friedman's work==
For a [[countable set|countable]] label set <math>X</math>, Kruskal's tree theorem can be expressed and proven using [[second-order arithmetic]]. However, like [[Goodstein's theorem]] or the [[Paris–Harrington theorem]], some special cases and variants of the theorem can be expressed in subsystems of second-order arithmetic much weaker than the subsystems where they can be proved. This was first observed by [[Harvey Friedman (mathematician)|Harvey Friedman]] in the early 1980s, an early success of the {{nowrap|then-nascent}} field of reverse mathematics. In the case where the trees above are taken to be unlabeled (that is, in the case where <math>X</math> has size one), Friedman found that the result was unprovable in [[arithmetical transfinite recursion|ATR<sub>0</sub>]],<ref>{{harvnb|Simpson|1985|at=Theorem 1.8}}</ref> thus giving the first example of a [[impredicativity|predicative]] result with a provably impredicative proof.<ref>{{harvnb|Friedman|2002|p=60}}</ref> This case of the theorem is still provable by Π{{su|p=1|b=1}}-CA<sub>0</sub>, but by adding a "gap condition"<ref>{{harvnb|Simpson|1985|at=Definition 4.1}}</ref> to the definition of the order on trees above, he found a natural variation of the theorem unprovable in this system.<ref>{{harvnb|Simpson|1985|at=Theorem 5.14}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Marcone|2005|pp=8–9}}</ref> Much later, the Robertson–Seymour theorem would give another theorem unprovable by Π{{su|p=1|b=1}}-CA<sub>0</sub>.

[[Ordinal analysis]] confirms the strength of Kruskal's theorem, with the [[proof-theoretic ordinal]] of the theorem equaling the [[small Veblen ordinal]] (sometimes confused with the smaller [[Ackermann ordinal]]).{{sfn|Rathjen|Weiermann|1993}} Kruskal's tree theorem itself proves that <math>\Gamma_0</math>, the [[Feferman–Schütte ordinal]], is [[well-founded]]; in particular, the inf-embeddable ordering on a countable label set contains a well-ordered chain of order type <math>\Gamma_0</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Gallier|1991|at=Theorem 9.2}}</ref>

==Weak tree function==
Suppose that <math>P(n)</math> is the statement:

:There is some <math>m</math> such that if <math>T_1, \ldots, T_m</math> is a finite sequence of unlabeled rooted trees where <math>T_i</math> has <math>i+n</math> vertices, then <math>T_i \leq T_j</math> for some <math>i<j</math>.

All the statements <math>P(n)</math> are true as a consequence of Kruskal's theorem and [[Kőnig's lemma]]. For each <math>n</math>, [[Peano axioms|Peano arithmetic]] can prove that <math>P(n)</math> is true, but Peano arithmetic cannot prove the statement "<math>P(n)</math> is true for all <math>n</math>".<ref name="SmiA">{{harvnb|Smith|1985|p=120}}</ref>  Moreover, the length of the shortest [[formal proof|proof]] of <math>P(n)</math> in Peano arithmetic grows phenomenally fast as a function of <math>n</math>, far faster than any [[primitive recursive function]] or the [[Ackermann function]], for example.{{citation needed|date=May 2023}} The least <math>m</math> for which <math>P(n)</math> holds similarly grows extremely quickly with <math>n</math>.

Friedman defined the following function, which is a weaker version of the TREE function below. For a positive [[integer]] <math>n</math>, take <math>\text{FFF}(n)</math> to be the largest <math>m</math> so that we have the following:

: There is a sequence <math>T_1, \ldots, T_m</math> of rooted trees, where each <math>T_i</math> has <math>i+n-1</math> vertices, such that <math>T_i \leq T_j</math> does not hold for any <math>i<j\leq m</math>.

Friedman computes the first few terms of this sequence as <math>\text{FFF}(1)=1</math>, <math>\text{FFF}(2)=2</math>, and <math>\text{FFF}(3)=5</math>. He also estimates <math>\text{FFF}(4)</math> to be less than 100, while <math>\text{FFF}(5)</math> suddenly explodes to a very large value. Any proof that <math>\text{FFF}(5)</math> exists in Peano arithmetic requires at least <math>A(10)</math> symbols, where <math>A(n)</math> is the unary version of the [[Ackermann function]], but it can be proved to exist in [[arithmetical comprehension|ACA<sub>0</sub>]] with at most 10,000 symbols.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Friedman |first1=Harvey |date=22 June 2006 |title=289:Integer Thresholds in FFF |url=https://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2006-June/010627.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240228223350/https://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2006-June/010627.html |archive-date=28 February 2024 |website=[[Ohio State University]] Department of Mathematics}}</ref>

==TREE function==
[[File:TREE(3) sequence.png|thumb|alt=Sequence of trees where each node is colored either green, red, blue|A sequence of rooted trees labelled from a set of 3 labels (blue < red < green). The <math>n</math>th tree in the sequence contains at most <math>n</math> vertices, and no tree is inf-embeddable within any later tree in the sequence. <math>\text{TREE}(3)</math> is defined to be the longest possible length of such a sequence.]]

By incorporating labels, Friedman defined a far faster-growing function.<ref name="TREE">{{Cite web |last=Friedman |first=Harvey |date=28 March 2006 |title=273:Sigma01/optimal/size |url=http://www.cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2006-March/010279.html |access-date=8 August 2017 |website=[[Ohio State University]] Department of Maths |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240918084441/https://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2006-March/010279.html |archive-date=18 Sep 2024}}</ref> For a positive [[integer]] <math>n</math>, take <math>\text{TREE}(n)</math>{{ref label|TR|a|^ a}} to be the largest <math>m</math> so that we have the following:

: There is a sequence <math>T_1, \ldots, T_m</math> of rooted trees labelled from a set of <math>n</math> labels, where each <math>T_i</math> has at most <math>i</math> vertices, such that <math>T_i \leq T_j</math> does not hold for any <math>i<j\leq m</math>.

Kruskal's theorem asserts that <math>\text{TREE}(n)</math> is finite for all <math>n</math>. The TREE function eventually dominates every provably recursive function of the system ACA<sub>0</sub> + Π{{su|p=1|b=2}}-BI.<ref name="TREE" /> It grows far faster than <math>f_{\Gamma_0}(n)</math> on the [[fast-growing hierarchy]]; Friedman calculated the ordinal <math>\alpha</math> where <math>\text{TREE}(n)</math> and <math>f_\alpha(n)</math> have similar growth rate (under [[affine transformation]] of input variables).<ref>{{harvnb|Gallier|1991|p=62}}</ref>

The sequence begins <math>\text{TREE}(1)=1</math>, <math>\text{TREE}(2)=3</math>; before <math>\text{TREE}(3)</math> increases to a value so large that many other "large" combinatorial constants, such as Friedman's <math>n(4)</math> and [[Graham's number]],{{ref label|n_k|b|^ b}} are surpassed by comparison. A [[lower bound]] for <math>n(4)</math>, and, hence, an ''extremely'' weak lower bound for <math>\text{TREE}(3)</math>, is <math>A^{A(187196)}(1)</math>,{{ref label|iteration|c|^ c}} where <math>A(x)</math> is the single-argument version of [[Ackermann's function]], defined as <math>A(x)=A(x,x)</math>.<ref name="TREE" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Friedman |first=Harvey M. |date=1 June 2000 |title=Enormous Integers In Real Life |url=https://u.osu.edu/friedman.8/files/2014/01/EnormousInt.12pt.6_1_00-23kmig3.pdf |access-date=8 August 2017 |website=[[Ohio State University]]}}</ref>

Friedman showed that <math>\text{TREE}(3)</math> is greater than the halting time of any [[Turing machine]] that can be proved to halt in ACA<sub>0</sub> + Π{{su|p=1|b=2}}-BI with at most <math>2\uparrow\uparrow1000</math> symbols,{{ref label|tetration|d|^ d}} where <math>\uparrow\uparrow</math> denotes [[tetration]].<ref name="TREE" />

==Notes==
:{{note label|TR|a|^ a}} Friedman originally denoted this function by <math>\text{TR}[n]</math>.
:{{note label|n_k|b|^ b}} <math>n(k)</math> is defined as the length of the longest possible sequence that can be constructed with a <math>k</math>-letter alphabet such that no block of letters <math>x_i,\ldots,x_{2i}</math> is a subsequence of any later block <math>x_j,\ldots,x_{2j}</math>.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Friedman |first=Harvey M. |date=8 October 1998 |title=Long Finite Sequences |url=https://u.osu.edu/friedman.8/files/2014/01/LongFinSeq98-2f0wmq3.pdf |access-date=8 August 2017 |website=[[Ohio State University]] Department of Mathematics |pages=5, 48 (Thm.6.8)}}</ref> For example <math>n(1) = 3</math>, <math>n(2) = 11</math>,  and <math>n(3) > 2 \uparrow^{7197} 158386</math>.
:{{note label|iteration|c|^ c}} The superscript indicates [[iteration]]. For example, <math>A^{3}(1)</math> would mean computing <math>A(A(A(1)))</math>.
:{{note label|tetration|d|^ d}} Friedman actually writes this as 2<sup>[1000]</sup>, which denotes an exponential stack of 2's of height 1000 using his notation.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Friedman |first1=Harvey |title=[FOM] 271:Clarification of Smith Article |url=https://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2006-March/010244.html |website=[[Ohio State University]] Department of Mathematics |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240226072403/https://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2006-March/010244.html |archive-date=26 Feb 2024}}</ref>
